title: Injection tests show that 1 in 7.6 million Gaia DR3 dwarf-band stars (95 %: 1 in 63 to 1 in 2.1 million) is in a Gaia20cdd-like deep-dimming state; ASAS-SN cannot test the south fainter than G = 16
abstract: Prior campaign searches found two kinematically old K-type field stars with deep, aperiodic dust dimming (Gaia20cdd and Gaia DR3 2870538750879109504) but did not measure their completeness. We reproduced the prior Gaia DR3 search exactly (4,559 candidates from 47.06 million dwarf-band stars) and completed its follow-up with IRSA ZTF DR24 and ASAS-SN Sky Patrol v2 for 684 northern candidates without ZTF answers and 1,296 southern candidates. We then simulated the full search for 20,000 random parent stars: the Gaia stage uses real DR3 transit times from the commanded scanning law, and the light-curve stage injects dimming into real ZTF and ASAS-SN light curves and runs the fixed search rules (1.66 million Gaia realizations, 21,300 light-curve injections). The Gaia scatter model reproduces Gaia20cdd (predicted 0.312, DR3 0.291). A star with the 2018-2025 dimming history of Gaia20cdd passes the Gaia stage with probability 0.75-0.81. ZTF recovers 73 percent of such stars, but ASAS-SN recovers 39 percent at G < 15 and none at G > 16, and it misses all four known dimmers at G = 16.0-17.4. The completed follow-up flags 9 stars; vetting assigns them to a young-star region, bright neighbours, single-camera ASAS-SN artefacts, or 'unclear' (one star), so no new member is found. The search equals a complete test of 15.3 million stars. With two members, the fraction of dwarf-band stars (G = 11-18.5, |b| > 10 deg) in a long-lived Gaia20cdd-like state is 1.3e-7 (95 percent: 1.6e-8 to 4.7e-7), about 6 (0.7-22) stars in the whole band. The onset rate is at most 1.5e-8 per star per year if activity lasts at least 9 years, at least 64 times below the campaign white-dwarf rate. For a 1-5 percent sky cover of the dust, 2.6e-6 to 1.3e-5 of stars host such dust, below the 1e-4 of old stars with bright warm dust, so these systems can be a subset of that population. Limitations: two detections, persistent activity only, one empirical template, assumed vetting success, our ASAS-SN artefact rules, and no spectra.
